Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
I distract myself with something else
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: For a 64-year-old male politician whose trauma was as a relief worker in a war zone, this self-harm item is the only clearly incoherent element. The rest of the profile depicts classic war-related PTSD with sensory/social triggers, intrusive fragmented memories, and hypervigilant threat monitoring, plus avoidance/emotion-control strategies. In contrast, deliberate physical self-harm as a distraction is not supported by the surrounding pattern: there are no negative appraisal items suggesting self-punishment, shame, or self-directed hostility, and the formulation shows strong Triggers→Maladaptive Strategies links that are better matched by distraction and emotion-control than by self-injury. This item is not impossible, but within this profile it is the one element a clinician would most question as belonging to the same patient formulation.

vignette: Elias had been coordinating medical supplies in a makeshift triage tent when the convoy engine backfired and the fuel lines ruptured. A thick, acrid cloud of burnt rubber and oil rolled through the canvas openings. He remembered the sudden drop in ambient noise as the dust settled, a heavy quiet that pressed against his eardrums. Then the voices returned, sharp and close. The memories did not arrive as a continuous story; they arrived as sharp, disconnected flashes: the cracked asphalt, the weight of a sandbag, the smell of scorched canvas, the rigid posture of a junior sergeant. He had come to believe that the moment never truly ended, that the war zone was still breathing around him. Weeks after returning to his duties as a state representative, Elias found his daily routine fracturing. He began scanning the perimeter of his district office before entering, his eyes moving from the reception desk to the heavy oak doors, then to the windows, making sure each latch clicked into place. He checked them again before lunch, and a third time before his evening staff meeting. The door and lock checking settled into a quiet ritual, a way to anchor himself. At the same time, he threw himself into legislative sessions and committee hearings, overworking to keep his mind occupied. He distracted himself with file folders and drafting amendments, but the quiet between committee members’ remarks began to feel loaded. An unusual silence in the chamber made him certain that something dangerous was about to happen, so he would shift in his seat, fingers resting lightly on the edge of his desk. When constituents approached him on the campaign trail or at public forums, Elias felt the familiar tightening in his chest. He forced himself to answer questions, but talking to strangers left him carefully measured, as if a wrong word might pull him backward. Military topics in the news or in casual conversation acted as a quiet alarm; when a reporter asked about defense appropriations or a colleague mentioned a recent deployment, Elias would feel the old tension return to his shoulders. A burnt smell from a nearby café grinder or a passing truck would stop him mid-step, the same terror he had felt in the tent rushing through his veins. He learned to control his breathing and keep his face steady, trying hard to control his emotions so he would not reveal how exposed he felt. The memories did not stay tucked away. During a quiet moment in his office, they would surface, bringing back the same terror he had felt at the time. When the overwhelm took him, he had to stop, resting his hands on the desk until the wave passed. Over months, his overworking and distraction had settled into a steady rhythm, and he would routinely skip evening briefings to finish drafting amendments. His divorce had long since settled into a quiet routine, but the weight of his daily vigilance had made him withdrawn. He was not afraid of the past itself, but of its sudden return, of the silence that felt like a warning, of the burnt scent that meant the ground was still shifting. What finally brought Elias to seek help was a district town hall where the room fell quiet during a question about local emergency preparedness. The silence stretched, his scanning tightened, and the heavy scent of floor wax mixed with the faint odors of the crowd. He felt the old terror rise, but this time he did not look away. He had come to hope that a therapist might help him carry the fragmented pieces without being pulled under, that he might sit with the quiet without bracing for impact, and that he might step through his office doors without checking the locks a third time.
